title: Auto-exposure for every token
allegory: LayerNorm is like auto-exposure on every photo: each token's vector has its own average brightness subtracted and its contrast set to a standard, then the studio's fixed colour grade is applied, so a dark shot and a bright shot of the same scene come out the same.
map: one token's residual vector, d_model numbers
set the contrast to a standard range
the studio's colour grade, applied after
learned gain w and bias b, one per feature
the exposure dial depends on the photo itself
the scale 1/√(var + ε) depends on x, so LayerNorm is not linear

chapters.name: Numbers adrift
chapters.note: every layer adds to the pile ... how big is it now?

cap.1: A transformer keeps a running total for every word, and each layer adds to it. The numbers the next layer reads could drift to almost any size.
cap.2: Each sublayer reads the residual stream, a d_model vector per token that every earlier layer has added into. Without a reset, the scale it sees varies by token and by layer.
cap.3: Sublayers are linear maps plus nonlinearities that work best in a particular input range. LayerNorm re-centres and re-scales each position's vector before it is read.

cap.1: Think of auto-exposure on a camera. A dark shot and a bright shot of the same scene come out looking the same. Then the studio adds its house colour grade.
cap.2: LayerNorm does this per token: shift the vector so its average is 0, scale it so its spread is 1, then apply a learned per-feature gain w and bias b.
cap.3: Per position: y = (x - μ)/√(σ² + ε) · w + b, with μ and σ² over d_model. Invariant to adding a constant to every feature and to positive rescaling of x (up to ε).

cap.1: Three moves: subtract the average, divide by the spread, then apply the learned grade. The average and spread come from this one token only.
cap.2: Mean and variance are taken over the d_model axis of one token. w and b are learned vectors of length d_model, so each feature gets its own gain and tint.
cap.3: Divide by (var + eps).sqrt() with unbiased=False, not by std + eps. They agree to first order, so the wrong one passes a loose check and fails GPT-2's reference comparison.

cap.1: Whatever size of numbers comes in, about the same size goes out. Tiny inputs get turned up, huge ones turned down, like auto-exposure.
cap.2: After LayerNorm (before w and b) the spread is about 1 whatever the input's spread. The exception is near zero, where ε stops the division from blowing up.
cap.3: Output std = σ/√(σ² + ε) → 1 once σ² ≫ ε (ε exaggerated here). The per-token gain 1/√(σ² + ε) is itself a function of x: the source of LayerNorm's nonlinearity.

chapters.name: Before, not after

left.title: Post-LN (2017 original)
lines: big gradients near the output at init

chapters.verdict: Normalise the reader's copy, never the running total.

cap.1: Where you put the exposure step matters. Normalise the running total itself and early training blows up unless you creep the learning rate up slowly.
cap.2: GPT-2 is Pre-LN: x = x + attn(ln1(x)). LayerNorm normalises what each sublayer reads and never touches the residual stream itself.
cap.3: Xiong et al. (ICML 2020), via mean field theory: Post-LN has large expected gradients near the output at init, so warmup was damage control. Pre-LN removes the cause.

cap.1: To read a model's insides, the house grade is easy to remove: it merges into the next step. The exposure dial is not, because it changes with every token.
cap.2: w and b are linear and always followed by a linear map, so TransformerLens folds them in with fold_ln=True. The divide by each token's own spread cannot be folded.
cap.3: Freeze the per-token scale and the rest is linear: DLA and QK/OV arithmetic apply that frozen scale by hand. Fine for small perturbations; an edit that shifts the norm breaks it.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Every block normalises what it reads
Steering edits pass through the dial

cap.1: Every block you build starts by normalising what it reads. When you later read or nudge a model's insides, remember this dial sits in the way.
cap.2: Build it once in [1.1], then meet it in every interpretability tool: folded weights, the scale factor in logit attribution, and cached 'normalized' activations.
cap.3: A steering vector added to the residual stream is rescaled with everything else by the next LayerNorm, so an edit's size is judged relative to that token's own norm.

coda.title: One token after LayerNorm: drag the input's scale and shift, then the learned gain
coda.f: (xs => xs.map(u => g * (u - mean(xs)) / sqrt(mean(xs.map(t => (t - mean(xs)) ** 2)) + 1e-5)))([2, -1, 0.5, -2, 0.5].map(v => a*v + shift))

caption.1: Drag the input's scale and shift: the input numbers swing wildly, but the bars stay put. Only the learned gain moves them. That is auto-exposure.
caption.2: Size and offset are thrown away; only the pattern across features survives. Drag scale down near 0.001 and the bars finally shrink: that is ε preventing a divide by zero.
caption.3: LN(a·x + c) = LN(x) for a > 0 while a²σ² ≫ ε; with ε = 1e-5 it fails only for tiny inputs. The gain here is one shared number; real LayerNorm learns one per feature.

where_else: BatchNorm in the [0.2] ResNet: the same shift and scale, but per feature across the batch, with train and eval modes
TransformerLens's fold_ln, and the scale factor you apply by hand in direct logit attribution
RMSNorm in newer models, which skips the centring and divides by the root-mean-square
Cosine similarity, which also keeps direction and throws away length

hamming.what: A per-token reset that shifts each residual vector to mean zero and unit spread, then applies a learned gain and bias.
hamming.when: Before every attention and MLP sublayer, and before the unembedding, in GPT-style transformers.
hamming.why: It keeps every layer's input in a sane range whatever earlier layers added, which steadies training; its input-dependent scale is why interpretability tools must fold or freeze it.

object.title: The exposure ring
object.subtitle: With three features, every normalised token lands on one ring inside the tilted plane where the features sum to zero.

cap.1: Three tokens, each just three numbers here: one tiny, one ordinary, one huge and shifted. Real tokens have hundreds of numbers, but the geometry is the same.
cap.2: Three raw residual vectors with d_model = 3, at very different scales and offsets.
cap.3: Raw inputs x ∈ R³; LayerNorm will act on each independently.

cap.1: Step one, subtract the average: each token drops onto the tilted plane where its three numbers sum to zero.
cap.2: Centring projects every vector onto the plane perpendicular to the all-ones direction.
cap.3: x - μ·1 is the orthogonal projection onto 1⊥, a (d-1)-dimensional subspace.

cap.1: Step two, divide by the spread: each token slides out or in from the centre until it sits on the ring. Tiny and huge end up the same size.
cap.2: Dividing by the spread puts every token at the same distance from the centre, whatever its original size.
cap.3: Dividing by the std maps every centred vector to norm √d (drawn smaller here to fit): a sphere inside 1⊥.

cap.1: All that survives is where on the ring a token sits: which features are high and which are low. Overall size and offset are gone.
cap.2: Only direction within the plane is kept. That is why a steering edit's effect depends on its size relative to the token's norm.
cap.3: LN (before w, b) is a radial projection onto a sphere in 1⊥: information about ‖x - μ1‖ and μ is discarded.

cap.1: Then the learned gain and bias stretch and move the whole ring, the same way for every token. That part is simple, and it can be folded away.
cap.2: w and b are one fixed linear map plus a shift, identical for all tokens, so fold_ln can merge them into the next weight matrix.
cap.3: The affine part diag(w)·y + b composes with the following W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_in or W_U; only the radial projection resists folding.

predict.q: Token B is token A multiplied by 10. After LayerNorm (before w and b), how do they compare?
predict.why: Dividing by the token's own spread cancels any positive overall scale (ε aside).

predict.q: Which part of LayerNorm can TransformerLens fold into the next weight matrix?

options.t: The divide by each token's spread

predict.why: The gain and bias are fixed linear pieces; the divide depends on each token, so it cannot be baked into weights.

predict.q: In GPT-2, does LayerNorm change the residual stream itself?

options.t: No, it normalises the copy each sublayer reads

predict.why: Pre-LN: x = x + attn(ln1(x)). The running total is never normalised in place.

object.where: Anywhere you keep a direction and discard its size: cosine similarity, RMSNorm, unit-normalised embeddings.
